2. This petition has been filed for quashing the order dated 18.05.2018 passed in Argora P.S. Case
No. 86 of 2018 (arising out of Complaint Case No. 698 of 2018), corresponding to G.R. Case No.
1906 of 2018, pending in the court of learned Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Ranchi.

3.  Mr. Jitendra Shankar Singh, learned counsel for the petitioner submits earlier complaint was filed which was sent under section 156(3) Cr.P.C. by the learned court pursuant to which F.I.R. was registered.

He submits that till date investigation is not completed and thereafter the petitioner has filed I.A. No. 1598 of 2024 challenging the F.I.R. as well as entire criminal proceeding which was allowed vide order dated 15.02.2024 and on that day the matter was adjourned on the prayer of the learned counsel for the informant to take instruction and file counter-affidavit 4.

Initially complaint case was filed which was sent under section 156(3) Cr.P.C. and pursuant to that F.I.R. has been lodged wherein it is alleged that Parijat Vyapar Private Limited is a corporate body dealing with the business of mining.

It is further alleged that accused no.1 and 2 entered into agreement of partnership with accused no.
3 for the purpose of operating the machines and dumpers.

It is further averred in the complaint that the complainant had some business transaction with the accused persons and he was entitled to get Rs. 3.95 Lacs from the accused no. 1 and 2.

On 30.01.2003 the accused no. 1, 2 and 3 entered into a memorandum of understanding with the complainant and the witness no. 1 and the said MOU was executed on 30.11.2003 at Ranchi amongst all of them by virtue of which it was made clear that the complainant was entitled to get Rs.
3.95 Lacs from the accused persons and it was further agreed that the said amount would be recovered till July 2003 from operation of CK-90 Machine from accused no.2 (petitioner herein),
Monthly hire charge of machine was also fixed to the tune of Rs. 1.75 Lacs per month.
The further condition of MOU was in respect of returning machine to accused no. 2 (petitioner herein) subject to adjustment of Rs. 3.95 lacs payable to the complainant.
It is also alleged that the said machine was not working properly and the complainant used to press hard for refund of his money of Rs.3.95 lacs.

On 29.12.2003 complainant wrote a letter to the accused no. 1 and 2 stating inter- alia that accused persons did not comply by their promise and as a result whereof the complainant's work was badly affected.
It has also been alleged in the complaint that the said machine was never delivered to complainant rather accused no. 3 was the custodian of the same.
It is further alleged that behind the back of the complainant the said machine was taken away by the accused persons but the outstanding amount of Rs. 3.95 lacs was not paid to the complainant.

5. Mr. Jitendra Shankar Singh, learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner resides at Kolkatta where in the complaint petition address of the petitioner has been provided at Ranchi.
He submits that the 41-A Cr.P.C. notice was alleged to be served at Ranchi but the petitioner has not received the said notice.
He submits that allegations are made that for non functioning of machine supplied by the petitioner on rent to the complainant.

Learned counsel for the petitioner further submits that when the rent of the said machine was not being paid and the machine was also not returned, the petitioner moved before the Calcutta High Court by way of C.S. No. 323 of 2003 and the said case was allowed in favour of the petitioner by decree dated 06.08.2009.
He further submits that an Execution Case No. 21 of 2010 was also filed and for non compliance of decree five properties of the informant was attached by the competent executive court.

He further submits that thereafter present petitioner filed W.P.(C) No. 5776 of 2010 as execution case was dismissed and the said writ petition was allowed by order dated 12.12.2017 in favour of the present petitioner.

He further submits that informant challenged the judgment and decree before the Hon'ble Division Bench of Calcutta High Court in APOT No. 244 of 2015 and the same was dismissed by order dated 24.08.2015.

He further submits that against said judgement of the Calcutta High Court the informant moved before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Special Leave to Appeal (C) No. 28394 of 2015 and the said S.L.P. was dismissed by order dated 08.08.2017 with cost.

sentences.text: "10. By non-disclosure the respondent has, in troth, concealed the existence of a pending civil suit between him and the appellants herein before a competent civil court which obviously is the causative incident for the respondent's allegation of perpetration of the aforesaid offences against the appellants.
We will deal with it further and also its impact a little later.

There cannot be any doubt with respect to the position that in order to cause registration of an F.I.R. and consequential investigation based on the same the petition filed under Section 156(3), Cr.P.C., must satisfy the essential ingredients to attract the alleged offences.

In other words, if such allegations in the petition are vague and are not specific with respect to the alleged offences it cannot lead to an order for registration of an F.I.R. and investigation on the accusation of commission of the offences alleged.

As noticed hereinbefore, the respondent alleged commission of offences under Sections 323, 384, 406, 423, 467,
468, 420 and 120B, IPC against the appellants.

A bare perusal of the said allegation and the ingredients to attract them, as adverted to hereinbefore would reveal that the allegations are vague and they did not carry the essential ingredients to constitute the alleged offences.

There is absolutely no allegation in the complaint that the appellants herein had caused hurt on the respondent so also, they did not reveal a case that the appellants had intentionally put the respondent in fear of injury either to himself or another or by putting him under such fear or injury, dishonestly induced him to deliver any property or valuable security.
The same is the position with respect to the alleged offences punishable under Sections 406, 423, 467, 468, 420 and 120 B, IPC.

The ingredients to attract the alleged offence referred to hereinbefore and the nature of the allegations contained in the application filed by the respondent would undoubtedly make it clear that the respondent had failed to make specific allegation against the appellants herein in respect of the aforesaid offences.

The factual position thus would reveal that the genesis as also the purpose of criminal proceedings are nothing but the aforesaid incident and further that the dispute involved is essentially of civil nature.
The appellants and the respondents have given a cloak of criminal offence in the Issue.

In such circumstance when the respondent had already resorted to the available civil remedy and it is pending, gol going by the decision in Paramjit Batra (supra), the High Court would have quashed the criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court but for the concealment.

11. In the aforesaid circumstances, coupled with the fact that in respect of the issue Involved, which is of civil nature, the respondent had already approached the jurisdictional civil court by instituting a civil suit and it is pending, there can be no doubt with respect to the fact that the attempt on the part of the respondent is to use the criminal proceedings as weapon of harassment against the appellants.

The indisputable facts that the respondent has filed the pending title suit in the year 2015 he got no case that he obtained an interim relief against his removal from the office of Secretary of the School Managing Committee as also the trusteeship, that he filed the stated application for an order for investigation only in April, 2017 together with Mahesh Kejriwal @ Mahesh Kumar Kejriwal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 13 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116633048/

For all these reasons, we are of the considered view that this case invites invocation of the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR registered based on the direction of the Magistrate Court in the afore-stated application and all further proceeding in pursuance thereof.

Also, we have no hesitation to hold that permitting continuance of the criminal proceedings against the appellants in the aforesaid circumstances would result in abuse of the process of Court and also in miscarriage of justice."
6.

Relying on the aforesaid judgment, learned counsel for the petitioner submits that if the case is civil in nature criminal case is unwarranted and suppressing the facts criminal case has been filed against the petitioner.

He further submits that every breach of contract does not give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction, the entire criminal proceeding may be quashed.

7. Learned counsel for the State submits that on reference by the learned court under section 156(3)
Cr.P.C. the F.I.R. has been registered and investigation is still going on.

8. Learned counsel for the informant submits that High Courts are very slow in quashing the F.I.R.
if case is made out.

He further submits that notice under section 41-A Cr.P.C. has been received by the petitioner however wrong statement in para 7 and 9 of the petition has been made that petitioner has not received notice.
He further submits that machine was supplied however, the informant has not received the said machine.
Learned counsel for the informant relied in the case of Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Smt. Raj Kumari & Ors."

On these grounds, he submits that this petition is fit to be dismissed.
9. It is an admitted position that F.I.R. was registered by the police by the order of the learned court sent under section 156(3) of Cr.P.C.
The contents of complaint suggests that dispute revolves around for a machine.
The allegations are made that the machine was not working and in view of that rent was not paid.

It is an admitted position that so far filing of case before the Calcutta High Court as well as Division Court of that Court and before this Court in writ petition as well as before the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the informant has appeared in that cases however, he has suppressed in the complaint petition.

It is crystal clear that informant has not approached this Court with clean hands disclosing all these facts and suppressing filing of the Civil cases suggests that maliciously the present case has been filed against the petitioner.
In the civil case the dispute has already been decided and that has been affirmed upto the Hon'ble Supreme Court.
Thus, the contention of the learned counsel for the informant in not receiving the machine is not being accepted by this Court.

10. There is no doubt that High Courts are very slow in quashing the proceedings if case is made out but at the same time if a proceeding like this is brought to the notice of the court not exercising power under section 482 of Cr.P.C. will amount the abuse of process of law.

Further even the F.I.R.
can be quashed that is well settled law in view of judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana and others V. Bhajan Lal and others" 1992 Supp. (1) SCC 335 wherein para 102 it has been held as under:-

sentences.text: In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

(1) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.

(2) Where the allegations in the first information report and other materials, if any, accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.

(3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code.

(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

(6) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.

(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge."

11. The case of the petitioner is coming within guideline no.
102(7).
12.

Further it is well settled law that merely on the allegation of failure to keep up promise will not be enough to initiate criminal proceedings and further that breach of contract does not give rise to Mahesh Kejriwal @ Mahesh Kumar Kejriwal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 13 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/116633048/

criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction, the entire criminal proceeding can be quashed and the case is arising out of civil in nature that has already been finalized and to allow the proceeding will amount abuse of process of law.
13.

The case of the petitioner is covered in the light of judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Usha Chakraborty (supra).
14.

The judgment relied by the learned counsel for the informant in the case of Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd (supra) is arising out of Motor Vehicle Act and in that case judgment was passed observing that a decision is an authority for what it actually decides and not every observation found therein nor what logically flows from the various observations made in the judgment are required to be made.
This judgment is not helping the informant.

15. Accordingly, the order dated 18.05.2018 and entire criminal proceeding in connection with Argora P.S. Case No. 86 of 2018 (arising out of Complaint Case No. 698 of 2018), corresponding to G.R. Case No. 1906 of 2018, pending in the court of learned Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate,
Ranchi, is hereby quashed.
16. This petition is allowed and disposed of.
Pending I.A, if any, stands disposed of.
Interim order is vacated.

(Sanjay Kumar Dwivedi, J.) Satyarthi/AF.R.
